title: Find information for a real decision
text: Imagine a neighbor asks where they can get help using a computer. You may already have a familiar library, community center, or veterans' organization in mind. Use that experience as a starting point, then verify what is available now. Our task is to find a suitable public service, record enough evidence to revisit it, and organize a fictional handout without exposing private information. You can use a different local service that matters to you. The names and details in this demonstration are examples, not a claim about any particular organization. A useful search ends with a supported decision, not just a page that looks impressive.

title: Turn a broad question into a useful search
text: Start with the words that describe your task, the kind of service, and the location. Computer help library plus your town is more useful than typing help by itself. Inspect the result title and the website address before opening it. If the results are too broad, add a specific service or location. If there are no useful results, remove one restriction rather than assuming the service does not exist. Filters can help, but they can also hide a relevant page. Pause and write a search for your chosen community task. Explain what each word contributes. Then change one term and compare the results instead of opening every link.

title: Judge the source and the fit
text: A page can be accurate and still be wrong for your decision. An official library page from another town may describe a real service, but not the one available to your neighbor. Ask who published the information, what evidence supports it, when it was updated, why it was written, and whether it answers your question. For opening hours or eligibility, go to the organization responsible for that service and check the details there. Search-result snippets may be incomplete. Compare two pages that disagree. Do not count votes between websites; identify which source is in a position to know, and confirm uncertain details through an independently found contact method.

title: Leave a source trail for your future self
text: Suppose you find a useful service today and need it again next month. A note saying good website will not be enough. Record the organization, the page title, the web address, the date you checked it, and the particular fact you plan to use. A bookmark helps you return, but it does not freeze the page or prove that the information remains current. In your handout, distinguish a checked fact from your own interpretation. If the page does not answer a question, write needs confirmation rather than filling the gap with a guess. This is the digital equivalent of writing the source beside a number in a household notebook.

title: Fill a form with the minimum useful information
text: An online form is a structured request. Read its purpose and required fields before typing. In our course practice form, choose the kind of computer help needed and a fictional contact preference. Review the entries before selecting the final button. On a real service, ask whether a sensitive detail is necessary for the task, and verify the site before entering it. Our practice does not send a real request. That distinction matters: seeing a confirmation message in a simulator proves that you completed the exercise, not that an organization received anything. Pause, complete the fictional form, and explain what you deliberately left out and why.

title: Give your files a home you can recognize
text: Think of a folder as a labeled place to put related work. Create a practice folder for the community resource task and use a descriptive file name, such as library-help-draft. A file saved on this computer may not appear on another computer. A cloud file belongs to a service and an account, and a synced folder may keep copies in more than one place. Before moving to another device, check the account and the saving or syncing status. Reopen the file from the intended location. That simple test catches a common mistake: editing one copy while later opening an older copy somewhere else.

title: Choose access by what the partner must do
text: Our partner should suggest clearer wording without rewriting the handout directly. Viewer access usually allows reading. Commenter access, when supported, allows suggestions through comments. Editor access permits changes to the content. Choose the smallest role that fits the task, inspect the recipient carefully, and have the partner verify that the file opens with the expected controls. A link that works for you may still fail for someone else. Also distinguish read-only from encryption. Read-only limits editing; it does not necessarily prevent someone from reading or copying the information. Pause and choose a role for someone who only needs to read the finished handout. Viewer is the appropriate starting point.

title: Separate sync from a recovery copy
text: Sync is convenient because a change can travel between a device and an online service. The same convenience can carry a deletion. Watch the practice file disappear from one location and then the other. That is why sync alone is not a separate backup. A backup provides another recovery copy under an appropriate plan. Version history may preserve earlier content, while a recycle bin may retain a deleted file for a limited time. Availability and retention depend on the service. Do not test deletion with your only important file. Use the fictional copy and explain which protection would help if the mistake spread through every synced location.

title: Recover the right thing and package carefully
text: First identify the problem. If the whole file is missing after deletion, inspect the appropriate trash or recycle bin. If the file exists but its wording changed, inspect version history. Preview the earlier version and coordinate with collaborators before restoring it. You do not want to replace useful work someone just added. Compression is a separate tool: a ZIP file can package several files for transfer and may reduce their size. It is not automatically encryption or a backup plan. After extracting a practice ZIP, open a file to confirm the contents are usable. Choose the tool that matches the problem rather than trusting a familiar icon.

title: Show the evidence behind your choices
text: Pause and build a small resource folder for your chosen community task. Include a source note, a fictional handout, and a clear file name. Tell a partner which fact you verified, why that source is appropriate, and which permission fits the review task. Then explain how you would recover a deleted file and how that differs from restoring earlier wording. If an account or sharing feature is unavailable, demonstrate the decision with the course simulator and label it simulated. For your next independent task, reuse this sequence: ask a focused question, check the evidence, record a trail, organize the file, and verify access.
